title: The churches and the Holocaust
hook: Christians were among the silent and the complicit; a few, like the villagers of Le Chambon, hid Jews

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bonhoeffer's end and his last message: for me, the beginning of life.

A knock at a farmhouse door, high on a cold plateau in the south of France. Outside, a stranger with a small suitcase, sometimes a child with no parents at all. Inside, a Protestant farming family who know what it is to be hunted, because their church remembers a long history of persecution. They open the door. Across the plateau, around the village of Le Chambon-sur-Lignon, families did that again and again, hiding Jewish refugees in homes, farms and schools. This story has to be told next to a much harder one.

The hard story first, said plainly. The Nazi state and those who helped it murdered Jews across Europe on a scale that is hard to hold in the mind. It happened in countries full of churches. Christians were among the silent and among the complicit: people who looked away, people who informed, people who took part. Behind it lay a long history of Christian contempt for Jews, sermons and laws and slanders, including the false charge that the Jewish people as a whole were guilty of Jesus's death. Since the war, churches have said this out loud. The Catholic Church and other churches have formally rejected that charge, and some have asked forgiveness for the contempt that helped prepare the ground. Now the few. On the plateau, the pastor André Trocmé and his wife Magda helped lead their parish in sheltering refugees. Tradition says that when officials demanded names, the village answered that they didn't know any Jews, only people. Elsewhere there were others: a farmer, a nun, a bishop, a teenager carrying forged papers. Israel's Holocaust memorial, Yad Vashem, honors rescuers like these as Righteous Among the Nations, and it has honored the people of that plateau. The rescuers weren't the rule. That's why their names are known. An old proverb in the King James Bible names what they refused to do: "If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death, and those that are ready to be slain; If thou sayest, Behold, we knew it not; doth not he that pondereth the heart consider it?" We knew it not, people said afterward. The few who hid them could never say it. They opened the door knowing exactly what it might cost.

What do you know about the people who hid others in those years? Maybe a name, maybe nothing yet; either is a fair place to start. Let the hard part sit beside it, the people who were not hidden and the homes that stayed closed. If you pray, pray for the dead; if not, simply stay with both.
Le Chambon. The French plateau village where Protestant families sheltered Jewish refugees again and again during the Holocaust.
Your line: the few who hid them. They knew, and they opened the door. Day nine hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Some churches now keep Holocaust Remembrance Day or Yom HaShoah services, often with local Jewish communities, and teach their members the history of Christian anti-Judaism alongside the stories of rescuers.

chat.says: Did the churches mostly protect Jews during the Holocaust?
options: No. Christians were among the silent and complicit; rescuers like those at Le Chambon were few.
Yes. Most church members hid Jewish neighbors, and that's why the rescuers are famous.
Churches had no part in it either way; religion had nothing to do with what happened.
chat.meaning: The lesson tells the hard story plainly: Christians were among the silent and the complicit. The rescuers Yad Vashem honors weren't the rule.

Le Chambon-sur-Lignon.meaning: a village on a high plateau in southern France

Righteous Among the Nations.meaning: Yad Vashem's title for non-Jews who risked their lives to save Jews

André Trocmé.meaning: the pastor who helped lead the rescue on the plateau

complicit.meaning: sharing in a wrong by helping it happen

notes: Claims rule: no death toll is stated (the cited texts do not give one); the scale is described without a number.
The index hook's 'thousands' of Jews hidden at Le Chambon is not repeated (claims rule).
'Christians were among the silent and among the complicit' replaces the index's 'many Christians were silent or complicit'; the hook field is softened the same way and drops 'thousands'. Confirm.

'The Catholic Church and other churches have formally rejected that charge' (Nostra Aetate 4; many Protestant statements) and 'some have asked forgiveness' (e.g. We Remember, 1998; Lutheran statements on Luther's anti-Jewish writings). Confirm wording.
The line 'we don't know any Jews, only people' is a tradition about Le Chambon; framed as 'tradition says'. Confirm or cut.
Yad Vashem honored the inhabitants of the plateau collectively; confirm phrasing. The Trocmés are individually recognized; confirm.
Hebrew phrase spelling (חסידי אומות העולם) and pronunciation: confirm.
Tone: the hard history is told first and plainly, so the rescuers are not used to soften it. A Jewish reviewer's eye on this day would be welcome.
